newsitem.title: GERMANY: German banks hit by mass protests on sick pay.
newsitem.headline: German banks hit by mass protests on sick pay.

text.p: German bank workers on Friday staged nationwide industrial action against cuts by employers to sick pay entitlements, with some 40,000 workers in the sector due to take part in protests during day.

Around 800 bank workers demonstrated in front of Frankfurt's Alte Oper opera building, where German Chancellor Helmut Kohl and finance ministers from across Europe were speaking at the European Banking Congress.
Some 1,200 bank workers in the northern town of Hamburg had earlier abandoned their positions while 2,000 employees in the northern state of Schleswig-Holstein were also due to walk out.
Other industrial action ranging from temporary walk-outs to a possible day-long strike has been scheduled in around 20 German towns across the country.
The industrial action had been called to protest against a new law that has allowed employers to cut sick pay from 100 percent of salary to 80 percent.
"This is a slap in the face for employees," Claus Carlin, chief negotiator for the HBV banking and insurance employees union, said in a statement.

Gerd Renner, negotiator for the DAG white-collar workers union, added that German banks, which are seeking to gain more trade by extending their opening hours, were not the "almshouses of the nation".

Bank workers have traditionally been less inclined to industrial action than those in sectors such as the metal and engineering industry, which has already staged protests involving hundreds of thousands of workers.
But a number of major banks, including Deutsche Bank and Dresdner Bank have already implemented a new federal law allowing them to cut sick pay to 80 percent of workers' salaries.

Banking unions have argued that while wage contracts in the sector do not specifically cover sick pay at 100 percent of salary, the move to cut sick pay is unjustified and unnecessary because of the low absenteeism in the industry.
They add that contracts in the sector allow them to launch all-out strikes without the customary six-week notice period often required under German employment law.
